Moss: morning
What’s simmering this early?
Barley and onions. I start the pot before the carts arrive so the porters can eat something hot.
morning
Who gets the first bowl?
Whoever carried the water. Today that was Juniper, though she insists she was just passing.
day
What keeps well on the road?
A pear travels better than a bowl of stew. Ask Rowan which ones are ripe before you pack.
day
Why is that cutting board so scarred?
The old one split down the middle. Merrit made this one from the same door the stand used to have.
evening
Why are you keeping a bowl aside?
Lio comes off the harbour shift late. He says he never gets hungry, then finishes everything.
night
Still working?
The pot’s off. I’m counting bowls by touch because the lantern keeps attracting moths.
Rain
What do you cook on wet days?
Something you can eat with one hand. Everybody has the other one busy wringing out a sleeve.
Mist
Can you see the river from here?
No, but I can hear the boats. The crews call out before they reach the bend.
Clear
What’s drying in the sun?
Apple slices. If the wind holds, I’ll have enough to put a few in the road lunches.
Cloudy
Did the bread rise?
Slowly. I moved it nearer the stove and got on with chopping instead of staring at it.
weekend
Are weekends busier?
The anglers come back together. It gets quiet right before they arrive with six versions of the same story.
midweek
Do you go hear Wren play?
I catch the last song if the washing’s done. Sometimes Wren starts it again when they see me.
friend_morning
Did you always run the stand?
I borrowed a cooking pot from the watch and never returned it empty. Eventually they asked me to stay.
friend_day
What did the Oldwater crew teach you?
Salt the fish after it’s cooked. One of them made me try both ways before she’d explain.
friend_evening
Why do you make extra?
One winter I came in too late for supper. A guard gave me half his bread. I remember that every time I measure barley.
close
What would you cook for yourself?
The onion soup my brother used to make. He always burned the toast. Now I burn one slice on purpose.
bartle: morning
What are you stocking first?
Bandages and lamp oil. The things people forget tend to sell before breakfast.
day
Do I need to buy everything?
Pick the problem that ended your last run. Buy for that one and leave space for what you find.
evening
What do you do with the empty crates?
Perrin takes them on his morning round. I put the good ones on top so he doesn’t have to sort them.
night
Why count stock this late?
It’s the only time I can count past eight without somebody asking where the spare straps are.
Rain
What should stay dry in my pack?
Your bandages. Fold them inside a dry pouch before you put the pouch in the bag.
Mist
Does mist change what sells?
More oil, fewer maps. People already know the road. They’re worried about not seeing the next bend.
Clear
What’s on the counter outside?
The leather straps. They smell better after an hour in the sun, and I can spot the cracked ones.
Cloudy
Are you expecting a delivery?
The market cart should be here before the clouds break. Joss has a better sense of that than I do.
weekend
Who comes in on the weekend?
First-timers, mostly. I keep the cheap kit close so they don’t feel they need a veteran’s purse.
midweek
What are you repairing today?
A buckle that came back from the Grove. The owner swears it snapped when a guardian sneezed.
friend_morning
What did you forget at Deepwell?
Lamp oil. I laid three spare buckles on the rock hoping one of them would turn into a light.
friend_day
What’s the oldest thing here?
A dented tin from my first supply run. I still use it to hold loose buttons.
friend_evening
Did someone help you out of the mine?
Orrin handed me his lamp before he asked how I’d got there. I try to remember that order.
close
What makes a good day at the shop?
Someone comes back, puts the spare bandage on the counter, and tells me they didn’t need it.
Rowan: morning
What are you checking in the beds?
The soil under the leaves. The surface can look dry while the roots have all the water they need.
day
What can I grow for a trip?
Start with an Antidote Pear. Leave a space for it in your food slot when you come to harvest.
evening
Why are you tying up that branch?
The weight of the pears pulled it almost to the path. I’d rather prop it than lose the whole branch.
night
What’s still out this late?
Slugs. Put the lantern down by the bed and you’ll see who’s been taking bites.
Rain
Do you like the rain?
Up to a point. I moved the seed trays under the eaves so they don’t turn into little ponds.
Mist
Why do the leaves shine?
The mist beads at their tips. Wait a minute and you’ll see each one tip under the weight.
Clear
What’s in the paper envelopes?
Seeds drying in the sun. I write the name before I fill each one after a particularly confusing spring.
Cloudy
Do sprouts mind the shade?
For a little while it helps. I put the tender ones outside when the sun’s behind the clouds.
weekend
Do you still swap seeds?
When someone brings a cup of tea and time to sit. The best swaps happen after the work is finished.
midweek
Are those cuttings for the market?
Two for the market and one for Briar. I want to see what Briar does with it.
friend_morning
Where did the first pear come from?
A boat crew gave me two. I ate one on the dock and brought the other home in my coat.
friend_day
What’s in the borrowed garden?
Mint from Briar, a lake pear, and a bean whose giver insisted it needed a name. It’s called Hal.
friend_evening
Have you ever lost a whole crop?
Yes. I planted everything at once. A cold night taught me to leave half the seeds in the drawer.
close
Which bed should I look at first?
The little crooked one by the door. It’s where I put the plants people thought wouldn’t make it.
elder: morning
Do you always wake this early?
I like to hear the first wagon over the bridge before the square fills up.
day
What should I see before leaving?
Take a turn past the river. Knowing how to get home makes it easier to go somewhere new.
evening
Why stay by the portal?
Someone generally arrives with a question. In the evening it’s often where to get supper.
night
Does the portal get quieter?
The square does. You can hear the stone humming when nobody’s talking over it.
Rain
Did this square always flood?
Before the drain, yes. Merrit still tells the story of fishing a bench out of the gutter.
Mist
Can fog come through the portal?
I’ve watched folks step through soaked on a clear day. What follows them through is usually their own weather.
Clear
Where do you sit on a clear day?
The west bench, if I can get it. It’s the one from which you can see who’s coming up the road.
Cloudy
Is there a storm coming?
Ask someone who works outside. I keep losing that argument to Rowan.
weekend
Who comes back on the weekend?
The people who say they’re only stopping for supplies. They usually stay until the lamps go on.
midweek
What’s the song from the square?
Wren learned it from a ferryman. The ferry stopped running years ago, but the song still makes its rounds.
friend_morning
What was here before the shops?
A few canvas roofs and a stone well. The first thing we bought together was a second bucket.
friend_day
Did you have a favourite realm?
The Grove. I could walk one trail often enough to notice what had changed since the week before.
friend_evening
When did you decide to stay?
Someone left my usual chair out while I was gone. I’d never had a usual chair before.
close
Do you miss adventuring?
Sometimes. Then a new traveler tells me what they saw, and I get to picture a place I already know through their eyes.
reel: morning
Why check the water before opening?
I can tell which way the wind has been blowing by what’s caught against the dock.
day
Where should I cast first?
Try the sheltered side of the pilings. Watch where the current curves and carry your line across it.
evening
How was the catch today?
Small fish near the steps. Nell stayed late after seeing something bigger turn under the boards.
night
What do you hear past the docks?
Sometimes a boat, usually the ropes knocking against the posts. Give them room to move.
Rain
Would you fish in this rain?
From the bank, yes. I’d wait before taking a small boat out if the wind rose too.
Mist
How do the crews find the landing?
By the bell and each other’s voices. The first to tie up calls the rest in.
Clear
Why is the line stretched out?
Let it dry straight. Mine spent a whole week coiled wet once and never forgave me.
Cloudy
What bait are people asking for?
Something that moves. Brin keeps the best advice near the bait counter.
weekend
Do you fish on your day off?
Of course. I walk up to Oldwater so nobody asks me to mind their line.
midweek
Who repairs your nets?
Lio if there’s time. I return the favour by making tea just before the late shift.
friend_morning
How did you learn the river?
I walked it with my aunt when I was too small to handle a rod. She made me point out somewhere safe to land.
friend_day
What did you catch on your first trip?
A boot. My aunt helped me weigh it like a prize, then threw it into the rubbish when I went to get a bucket.
friend_evening
Was there a trip you turned back from?
The mist thickened by the river mouth. I’d promised fresh fish and brought everybody home hungry. I’d make the same call again.
close
What do you still want to catch?
I’d like to take my aunt out one more time. She could spend a whole afternoon without catching a thing and call it perfect.
Tessa: Clean wraps. The people who need them rarely arrive when I have both hands free.
Who taught you to set a splint?
A climber named Oak, who demonstrated how not to land first.
Wet sleeves are cold enough without sitting on wet wood. Come in and warm up.
Do you worry when the gate gets busy?
I worry when it goes quiet before everyone has come back. That’s when I put another kettle on.
How do you go home after a hard shift?
I walk the long way by the river. By the second bend I can hear something besides the clinic door.
apothecary: The first weight includes yesterday’s rain. Give them a little time near the window.
Can I make my own consumables?
Bring your ingredients to the counter. I’ll show you what keeps and what you should brew just before leaving.
It changes what I can pick. I keep the dried leaves for days like this.
A salve for Merrit’s hands. It worked, but he smelled like onions for a week.
Do you have a favourite recipe?
A tea that doesn’t cure anything. Mira and I drink it when we’ve both had enough of being useful.
Brin: Off the quiet side of the steps, before everyone else starts dropping tackle.
Why are the bait tins open?
I dry the empty ones between shifts. Fish are choosy, and so am I.
To pay attention to where the fish are moving, even when the first bite comes somewhere else.
If Lio wants a whole evening free, I stay. I get to hear the late boats coming in.
Lio: What keeps you awake on the late shift?
The bell, cold tea, and trying to guess how many boats are still out.
Ever lose sight of the landing?
Not from the stand, but I can lose the far post. That’s when I move the lantern to the end.
Do you ever fish after work?
Sometimes I stay for dawn. I’m usually too tired to mind where my line goes.
What’s the best part of the night shift?
When Brin turns up early and we have the whole landing to ourselves for a few minutes.
Wren: The old ferry song. I leave room after the last line for anyone who knows the missing verse.
Are you playing in the square tonight?
If the strings stay dry, yes. Ask for a song you can hum all the way home.
Do you get nervous before playing?
Only until somebody stops walking and listens. It helps if their back is turned.
Who taught you the ferry song?
My neighbour, who sang while mending nets. Her version took as long as the whole net.
exchange: Let me see a fresh face first. A good vein can look like mud until you break it open.
Why are the sacks off the floor?
Wet ore stains everything and throws the scale off. The last customer paid for a bucket’s worth of rain.
I miss knowing the name of each tunnel. I don’t miss waiting for my eyes to get used to daylight.
Do you keep any of the stones you buy?
Just one. Orrin dropped it in my pocket the day I opened this counter.
mine: Why tap the supports before work?
A loose wedge sounds different. It’s easier to fix before the carts start rolling.
Can you tell how deep you are?
The draft changes near the lower galleries. If it stops altogether, I turn back.
Did you lend Bartle a lamp?
I lent one to someone with no oil and more buckles than sense. You’ll have to ask Bartle about the rest.
Do you remember your first shift?
My hands shook so badly I spilled my tea. Nobody mentioned it, and someone poured me another.
Briar: Did the rain spoil your experiment?
It saved me a trip with the watering can and moved all my labels two beds downhill.
Which flowers survived the Coast wind?
The ones nearest the wall. I spent a month breeding tougher flowers when I should’ve built a smaller wall.
Mira: Mint from Briar. He said it was an experimental batch, which usually means he planted too much.
Who used to share your tea?
My neighbour from the old ferry road. She drank the first cup hot and let the second go cold while she talked.
Alden: Only as far as the bridge. I’ve learned the difference between an interesting detour and needing someone to come find me.
Have you ever found a new trail?
Once, behind a fallen tree. It led to somebody’s back door, so I asked permission before putting it on my map.
Pip: A peg puzzle. The wooden pieces swell in the rain, so today getting them out is the puzzle.
One Ada taught me. I can win it if she makes a mistake. I’m still waiting.
Clover: Moss starts the soup before anyone puts out a sign. Follow the smell and you’ll usually beat the crowd.
One thing I’ve never cooked. Juniper has rescued me from several of those decisions.
Flint: Can you fix a swollen door?
I can. First I have to stop its owner from shaving half an inch off while it’s wet.
A cart wheel that didn’t need repairing. I was thirteen and had just been given a hammer.
Hazel: What do you leave for the bees?
The little flowers under the beans. People keep trying to weed them for me.
Which plant was hardest to grow?
The pear by the wall. Once I stopped moving it to find the perfect spot, it did fine.
Theo: Ask me about the bridge toll that was paid with a goose. Leave time for the part where the goose gets a vote.
The bridge is real. Beyond that, I try to be fair to the people who are still here to correct me.
Nell: Can you fish without seeing the float?
I can feel a bite through the line if I hold it lightly. It took me a long time to stop gripping it so hard.
Have you ever let a big catch go?
One at Oldwater. It barely fit in my net, and once I’d seen it up close that was enough.
Rowe: Is this a good day for a walk?
Excellent, if you planned to have the path to yourself and weren’t particular about dry socks.
Why take the long road home?
There’s a bit where the town falls quiet. I like choosing when to turn back into it.
Fern: A ledger that someone used as a diary. The margin notes are much better than the numbers.
Where do the old books come from?
Some arrive from the lake. One was returned with a ferry ticket marking a page nobody had read for years.
Kit: A letter to someone who gets up later than I do. I’ve got time to do the long loop first.
Have you ever lost a parcel?
For half an hour. I’d delivered it to Tuck, who was busy looking for me to give it back.
Bram: Can you see the Coast today?
Only the far shore if you know where to look. The rooftops make it look closer than it is.
Why watch the cliffs after dark?
On clear nights I can see the fishing lights. It makes the whole town feel a little less far from the water.
Lark: A wagtail. Watch the tail after it lands, and you’ll be able to pick it out next time.
Which bird took longest to spot?
A kingfisher. Nell finally told me to stop staring at the water and look at the branch above it.
Juniper: What are you making for lunch?
Pear and onion flatbread. I tried it the other way round and used twice as many pears as I meant to.
How to taste the soup before reaching for more salt. I did it to be polite and then had to admit he was right.
Tess: Can you sketch in the fog?
It’s the easiest time to draw the tower. Everything I’d usually have to erase has already disappeared.
The seedhouse door. Rowan hung it inside and never told me I’d drawn the hinges on the wrong side.
Oak: Once the rock warms up. I’ve spent enough mornings trying to make stiff fingers hold on.
Yes. If I stop paying attention to that feeling, I go home and try again another day.
Ada: If Pip brings the board. I put the missing piece in his pocket yesterday, so he may be looking for it.
Leaving a piece alone when you can move it. It took me years to learn to wait.
Finch: Which map are you marking up?
The town one. It shows where the streets are; I’m adding where you can get out of the rain.
Half the alleys have moved since they were drawn. I like remembering who used to live at the other end.
Ash: What do you look for on the trail?
The edges of the gravel. They’re still there when you lose sight of the trees ahead.
Most days. But I’m glad when somebody asks where I’ve been when I get back.
